elements.quote: Despite advances made in curbing the global malaria burden since the 2000s, progress has stalled, in part due to a plateauing of the financing available to implement needed interventions. In 2020, approximately 3.3 billion USD was invested globally for malaria interventions, falling short of the targeted 6.8 billion USD set by the GTS, increasing the financial gap between desirable and actual investment.
elements.reason: The abstract background describes the current state of knowledge (progress stalling despite advances) and the key uncertainty/gap (financing shortfall), motivating the use of optimization models.

elements.quote: Models for malaria control optimization are used to disentangle the most efficient interventions or packages of interventions for inherently constrained budgets. This systematic review aimed to identify and characterise models for malaria control optimization for resource allocation in limited resource settings and assess their strengths and limitations.
elements.reason: The importance and need for the review are explained: constrained budgets create a need to identify efficient intervention packages, and the review aims to characterise available models and their limitations.
No retrieved evidence discusses prior similar systematic reviews or justifies the current review as an update or replication; no previous review is identified or cited.
This is a review of optimization models for resource allocation, not a review of intervention effects, so describing a mechanism of action of an intervention does not apply.
The review examines modelling studies rather than evaluating complex intervention effects directly; no logic model requirement is indicated by the retrieved evidence.

elements.quote: The research question for this review was ' Are there English-language publications in peer-reviewed scientific journals describing how models have been used to allocate resources for malaria interventions in limited resource settings?' The main aim of this review was to identify and characterize models for malaria control optimization for resource allocation in malaria control and elimination settings and to identify their strengths and limitations.
elements.reason: The objectives and a research question are explicitly stated (also in the abstract, text_2: 'This systematic review aimed to identify and characterise models for malaria control optimization...'), but no question-formulation framework (e.g., PICO, SPIDER) is used or referenced.

This is a review of optimization models for malaria resource allocation, not a review of intervention effects comparing interventions, so planned PICO-style comparisons do not apply. The inclusion criteria (text_7) confirm the focus on models rather than effect estimation.

elements.quote: Studies containing an optimization model (mathematical or statistical); (6) All studies with human Plasmodium species; (7) Studies with two or more interventions; (8) Cost data were used in combination with the model outputs; (9) Outcomes/health benefits were clearly stated and/or measured.
elements.reason: Inclusion criteria specify eligible study design (optimization models), population (irrespective of subgroups, human Plasmodium species), interventions (two or more), and outcome requirements; no specific follow-up requirement applies to modelling studies.
